utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we still have to tender the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is due from Mr. Donia. Could I please ask for the assistance of the registry? Madam Registrar, could you help us out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 368 -- P3683, report of Robert Donia, two binders and supporting material.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to that exhibit, there are some additional materials: P368A, which is the binding contain the open source material; P3683B, which is a videotape in six parts titled "Death of Yugoslavia." I have those at the bar table now. A copy has been provided to the Defence. P3683C, which is the audiotape of the speech by Radovan Karadzic. You may remember, Mr. President, the Defence wished us to tender that as well. The transcript is at tab 200 of binder number 1, so perhaps I could hand over those materials. "The Death of Yugoslavia" is footnote 15 of the open source volume. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Ierace. It is admitted in evidence. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, if you allow me to do so. After my learned colleague suggested for these records to be adopted, my learned colleague objected to the record and binder number 2/2. This is a record. We don't know whether it is of the 14th of May or of the 12th of May. Our objection relates to the authenticity of this record, given that we didn't have the opportunity of seeing the original of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to find out. Is that the meeting subsequent to the meeting -- I haven't got any materials with me at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, it is a record, the command of the 1st Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In brackets it says: The 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not being presented by General Galic, according to the testimony, is that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you: I don't remember that there were any specific questions as to the source of where it came from. Of course, I heard several questions about how this was drafted, but not as to the source and Mr. Donia found it. Is my recollection correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I understood Mr. Donia, the document which was used by Mr. Donia to write his expert report, these were documents that were given to him by the Prosecutor. The Defence had this document at an earlier date before Mr. Donia used it for his expert report. My learned colleagues disclosed it but the problem was that, at our meetings, we never spoke about the authenticity of the documents. So that we now find ourselves in a situation in which I would like to contest or object to the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any specific reasons why the Defence takes that it might not be an authentic -- a copy of an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is because at the head of the document it says, "The Command of the 1st Partisan Brigade." As far as we know, in that area, we had the 30th brigade and at the time General Galic was the commander of the 30th division. So with regard to the stamp and the signature by the person who is the -- who took the minutes, we have a line and it says "cap," and it has been struck out. We don't know what capacity that person was at the meeting because we can't see whether it was a captain 1st class or just a captain. We don't know who crossed this out on the last page of this record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a decision after the break specifically in respect of this document. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. President, could I just note that my recollection is that if one goes to the original of the document, that is the B/C/S version, one can see quite clearly a line through the "captain" in that document and, therefore, it appears that the transcript into the English language merely faithfully records that. In any event, a line through those words hardly raises an issue as to the accuracy of the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the P3683 and the annexes A, B, C are admitted, but a decision on the document just referred to by Ms. Pilipovic will be taken after the break. Madam Registrar,

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D99, judgment in B/C/S; Exhibit D99.1, English translation; Exhibit D100, B/C/S article entitled "Cunning Strategy, Sarajevo 1997", D100.1, English translation; Exhibit D101, article in B/C/S entitled "On People in Front of the Assembly are Shooting Our Snipers"; D101.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to Exhibit 100, I have no objection to the tender of the passage which is translated into English and, of course, the B/C/S passage which covers that. The document is some pages in length but there is only a translation of one paragraph, so I have no objection to that paragraph. In relation to Exhibit 101, I object to that tender. You may recall, it appears to be a magazine article relating to certain events on the 5th of April, and it was put to Mr. Donia that it contradicted his account in respect of events on the 6th of April. He then pointed out the discrepancy in the dates, and I think at that point it lost all potential relevance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, would you like to respond, perhaps first to D100.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with regard to document D100, the Defence has only had one part translated, the part from the book which is relevant with regard to Mr. Donia's testimony, since Mr. Donia didn't speak about the Patriotic League as a military organisation formed within the Party of Democratic Action. And the Defence didn't have other parts translated, so I am not sure which part my colleague is objecting to as far as the text from the book is concerned, that is to say, the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... it is not translated, as far as I understand. Yes. So it seems that the parties agree on what is tendered, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is fine. As far as document 101 is concerned, it is true that in the article it mentions the 5th of April and that Mr. Donia in his expert report spoke about the 6th of April. But in response to our question, Mr. Donia said that on the 5th of April, too, people gathered near the Assembly, around the Assembly, and that on that same date, the 5th of April, citizens were fired upon. So that this document supports Mr. Donia's allegations as well as what is stated in his expert report, that is to say that it was on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is an allegation of such, but Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think the most important point, Mr. President, is that there was no cross-examination pursued in relation to the documents so once the date discrepancy was established and, therefore, it lacks any probative value. There has to be more of a nexus, in my respectful submission, in order for a party to tender into evidence a hearsay document, than what we have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute between the parties that there has been shooting both on the 5th and the 6th of April? I mean, not on whether it is Juka Prazina or not but on whether there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No dispute on that, Mr. President, according to my recollection of the evidence of Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if there is no dispute on that, I think that that was mainly used to, well, as you said, to allege that certain people might have shot at the crowd at that very moment, and there has been no further cross-examination on that issue. It stopped after it was established that it was a different date. Of course, this leaves entirely -- it is entirely up to the Defence when presenting their case, if it is relevant, to come up with further details as far as what happened on the other dates. But we will give a decision after the break but we will take into consideration what the parties have made as their observations. I think then D100, there is no dispute as to what part should be admitted. So D100 and D1001 are admitted, that's just the passage, and we will give a decision after the break on D101. Madam Registrar, I think that was all. Yes. Now, Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. President, and that witness will be taken by Mr. Stamp. Before that occurs, Mr. President, you will recall that I handed up last week a fresh translation of a document that came in through the witness Trto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would now would be a convenient time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could do it right now. That was the new translation with the two dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There were some pages missing, or a page missing from the original translation. It's P1675, that is the exhibit number for the B/C/S document, and a translation was requested of the missing page and, in fact, we received in return a fresh translation of the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If it is accepted into evidence, I suggest that it be .2, so the .1 remains the original translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the first time the Defence receives the new translation or -- yes? So perhaps it is better to take a decision after the break. If, Ms. Pilipovic, or Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if there is any objection against it, I would first like to give you the opportunity to have a look at it and to study it. And the Chamber then also can have a look at it. Anything else, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President. Might I be excused during the evidence of the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp, is my understanding correct that your next witness will be Witness AI and that a pseudonym, voice and facial distortion is granted in respect of that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that the voice distortion, which is usually the most problematic, has been set by now so that we could proceed. Is that correct? Yes, Madam Registrar. Then if all the protective measures are effective, Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. AI, because that is how I will call you, protective measures are in effect in respect of you. That means that your face cannot be seen by the outside world. Your voice cannot be heard in its original sound by the outside world, and you will not be called by your name, but you will be called "Mr. AI." Mr. AI, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration, and the text of that declaration will now be handed out to you. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. AI, you will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Stamp. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. AI. Firstly --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, I am going to ask you to look at a document, and say nothing after you look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, may I have the witness shown P3682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. AI, by answering "yes" or "no," can you tell me if you see your name on the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you see your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you live in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And for how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: 45 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you live there during the period 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript, it just says "1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That perhaps is the French transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall being injured in a shelling incident in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall the date of this incident when you were injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: The 22nd of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the time you were injured, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I was returning from a search for food. I was going home. I was in Alipasino. It is part of the town. It is the Alipasin bridge or Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were returning home. Could you tell us how you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By what means were you travelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, I was on foot but Alipasino Polje consists of -- I live in "C" phase, and I was returning from "B" phase because that was the closest way to get to the "C" phase. And in that part, in the "C" phase, as I was returning home, I was wounded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly what happened? As you walked, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: The distance between the "B" and "C" phase, I was passing through the "B" phase and I was heading towards the "C" phase. When the first shells fell, I didn't see them but judging by the detonation, they were very near. It was in Alipasino Polje. I can't really say whether it was in "A" or "C" phase but -- because I didn't see them. There were explosions in front of me. In the parking place, there was children who were on sledges, because it was quiet that morning. There was no shooting that you could hear. When these two explosions occurred, they ran towards the entrances to the buildings, and I ran after them. They were a little in front of me, perhaps four or five metres in front of me. When that third shell fell on my left side, three, four, or five metres from me, the explosion threw me into the air. I fell down. I started crawling towards building, the entrance of the building, which was about five or six metres away from me. And I then felt, as I was crawling on the asphalt, I felt that I had problems in my -- in part of my face. I didn't realise that I had been wounded. But then I realised I was wounded. I lie down on my side and headed towards the building, and the tenants found me there. They came out to collect the wounded after the explosion of that shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say what happened to the children who were running towards the apartment building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: After the explosion, when I was hit by the shrapnel, I heard screams and groaning, and because they were in front of me so that part of the shrapnel hit them. I didn't see this, but I heard screaming, I heard groaning, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were you taken? Can you say where you taken by the residents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: The residents from the building took me to -- they put me in a car. I think it was a Golf. They put me and a boy in that car and then, as it is all in the immediate vicinity, that Golf took us to the hospital in Dobrinja, and from Dobrinja, we were transported to the Kosevo hospital because they weren't able to help us there. So we were then taken to the centre of the town to the Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you admitted at the Kosevo hospital and were you discharged that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I was admitted and there was surgical intervention. They operated on me that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say about how long you were admitted in the hospital for, approximately, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: The first time when I was wounded, when they were saving my life, I stayed about two months. The second time, I was in hospital for about a month, and the third time, when they were transplanting my rib, I stayed for about two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us where on your body received injuries or serious injuries, if any, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: A piece of shrapnel hit part of my face, right here, and damaged my whole jaw, and exited here right next to my shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you tell us briefly, if you can, the nature of your treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to repeat myself. They patched up this part. I was clinically dead by the time I was transported to hospital. That lasted for about an hour and a half. So the first thing they did was save my life. And they sewed me up. I am not an expert on medicine. The second time, they put some pins in to make my jaw straight, and the third time they transplanted my -- part of my rib, and because my jaw had been shattered. It was very difficult for me to put it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand. Could you tell us whether or not there are any effects on you physically still from that injury?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot chew so I cannot eat food normally. I can only swallow. I have to eat soft food, mushy food. The nerves in my face have been damaged so that I don't feel part of my face, and then when they were stretching my skin to cover that place, my skin is very brittle now and it is hard to stop any bleeding. I also have pains in my shoulder so I do not feel normal at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And psychologically, are there any psychological effects from this shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes, very severe consequences. I am constantly under sedation and under control. I am being monitored. It is a bit hard for me to talk about it all, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I want to take you back to the day of the incident. I am sorry to have to do so, but I just want us to go through one or two more aspects of it in detail. You were in "B" phase of Alipasino Polje, you said, when you heard two shells explode in the community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The first two shells that you heard explode, did you hear the shell being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No, not the first two. I didn't hear the first two being fired, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hear anything after those two explosions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Right after that I heard, as I was running, there was a kind of eerie silence, and then I heard the whiz of the third shell being fired, and immediately after that, it landed in my immediately vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you say about how long after you heard the first two shells explode did you hear the second one being fired -- sorry, did you hear the third shell which injured you being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, a minute and a half or two minutes, something like that. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said -- well, my translation says you said you heard the whiz sound of a shell being fired. Could you describe the sound you heard a little bit more, the sound of the third shell being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, I will try, as far as my jaw will allow me. It is like opening a bottle, but much louder. It's a kind of hiss.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you say where the sound of this third shell being fired came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, behind my back, from the part where Nedzarici is, there was a military barracks there as far as we knew before the war. During the war, we didn't even dare look in that direction. We were afraid to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This area of Nedzarici from which the sound of the fire of the third shell came, under the control of which part of the conflict was it? Was it the army of the Republika Srpska or the army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: It was under control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you heard the sound of the firing coming from Nedzarici. Was this the first time you ever heard the sound of a shell being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know it is difficult to speak, so if you could tell us briefly about your experience in hearing shells being fired before that incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well to put it briefly, the "C" and the "B" phases were in the immediate vicinity of Nedzarici and there was daily shelling. It entered our subconscious so that we got used to living with it and we learned to distinguish the sounds of various kinds of projectiles being fired because they also fired from tanks. We could see them from the windows of our flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said it was a quiet day. What do you mean by that? Was there any other shelling in the community that day or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, that morning it was like a miracle. It was a cold January day and you couldn't hear a single bullet. It was so quiet, so peaceful, you couldn't hear -- at least, I didn't hear any shelling or any bullets being fired or anywhere around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the weather like that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: It was a cold, sunny day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you recall about what time of the day the shelling occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, a little after 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how long after you heard the third shell being fired did the explosion occur, that is the explosion which injured you and the children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, around two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I rephrase that. Between -- can you give us, and I know it would be an approximation, an approximate time period between the firing of the third shell and the explosion of the third shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, not more than ten seconds. Well, it is very difficult to say. But ten seconds at the most, not even that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you say, if you can, precisely, which street you were on when you were injured or which apartment building you were running towards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I think it was called Klara Zetkin Street then. I am not sure of the house number, but I think it was 4. I think it was entrance number 4. They changed the names of the streets after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the children you saw, where were they playing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: They were playing outside the entrances 2 and 4. There was an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. area in front, a parking space, where they were sledging or sliding along, skating in their shoes on the -- that part of the parking lot. And I was walking towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive a letter of discharge when you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would you be able to recognise a copy of it, if you saw it again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, could the witness be shown P2183A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a copy of the letter of discharge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you see your name, your father's name, and your year of birth on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I apologise for interrupting the proceedings. But in the document that I have before me, it seems that there is a handwritten part on the back. I don't know if everyone has the same and I don't see -- I can't see that this has been translated, this handwritten part. There is something that might be a date. I am not sure. Could my colleague Stamp provide us with some clarifications, perhaps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, I see some illegible scrawl of about five or six characters on the back. I don't know if that is what my friend is referring to. This is on my copy. I don't know if his copy has anything else. I have the original from -- or as it ends here. If my friend would have a look at it. The scrawl which I described is there but it is not a part of the document that the Prosecution proposes to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have a solution. It is probably a copy of the signature which is on the back of -- on the front of this document, although it seems to be a different person who has signed. But, I think, Mr. President, this is the same signature as the one that we can find -- as the one that we see on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest that it is the signature in mirror and not -- it reads -- no. Yes, I see. It is not a mirror. I do see it. I also see very slightly the name just above the signature, which appears to be the same name as we find twice on the front side, "Piranic" and the signature seems to be approximately the same. It has the appearance of the same signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But what is even more troubling is that we can read something, but very difficulty -- with a lot of difficulty. We can read the name of the doctor "Biranic" or "Piranic" which is marked on the back. But we can see on the text below, I can make out the word date "dana," which means "day," but I don't know whether this is something that was translated or not. Apparently not, because at the end of the document that we have here, on the front, it has been translated as A1 under this number. But the lines that we see on the front of the document, and this is not a mirror image because we can see it quite clearly, these lines have not been translated. Could Mr. Stamp tell us why.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Most probably, as is apparent, it is because that area of the document is not legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might create a lot of problem for Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As I indicated, the original is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we first see whether it is of any help if Mr. Piletta-Zanin has a look at the original. Mr. Usher, could you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Certain things appear to be more legible on the original. There is a date to the left which perhaps indicates -- which is perhaps February 1995. But I am sure that with a good magnifying glass, a good translator should be in a position to do miracles, and I have no doubt that he will do so very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at the original, as well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I can see - and this is not the first time that this has happened - the document that was given to us at the time by the Prosecution consists only of one page, and as you can see, the other side has not been reproduced. So yet again, regardless of the importance of the text, we are being provided with elements which have only been partially reproduced. I don't think that this is quite normal. Whatever the length of the text in question, it has to be provided to the Defence. All the more so in that the document coming from the Prosecution was clear, given that we could see that there were two sides that were -- it was printed on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In general terms, I would say that documents tendered at trial should be the same as the documents disclosed to the Defence. There is a slight difference. So in general terms, I would agree, but I don't think at this very moment, having inspected the document and also the original -- at least the most original is in the hands of the Prosecution, that there would be a reason at this moment not to continue to examine the witness. Mr. Stamp, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, if the please you, Mr. President, Your Honours, is the examination-in-chief of this witness. I have nothing further at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to cross-examination the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we would like to examine the question of translation for a few seconds. Because it seems that the translation that we have just received is not the same as the one that was given to us at the time. So we would like to verify this. That will take a little time. I am very sorry, but it would take a few seconds

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few seconds is fine. Otherwise, I would suggest that you start to cross-examine the witness and then perhaps during the break that you finalise the inspection of the translation. If it is just a matter of seconds, then, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are a few slight differences, but we could start with the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have your medical document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That document contains the address where you used to live; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you lived at this address from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And from a considerable time before that. So that is an area that you have lived for a long time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, since 1981.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the medical document that you have provided, it says that on the 17th of October, 1994, when you were admitted, you were employed in [redacted] Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, from 1991 to 1995, whether you were also employed in that organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No. We were all put on stand-by because of the wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So in that period 1992, 1993, 1994, you were not employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No. I was on stand-by like most of the employees there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in April, May or June, did you receive a draft note?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- hesitate to hand. I am wondering if perhaps the questions dealing with the employment of the accused at a particular place might be sufficiently direct that it might disclose - I beg your pardon - the questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, Ms. Pilipovic, I think until now it is just a matter of whether the witness was employed or at stand-by. So that might be true perhaps for some more people in the area in these times. But Ms. Pilipovic, would you please keep in mind very much that also the identity of the witness is protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am obliged, Mr. President. And to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will endeavour to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you provided us with a document saying that you were admitted to hospital on the 17th of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you have documentation about your admission to hospital dating from January 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you confirm that you did not hand over these documents to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I can't remember. I gave them a lot of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are confirming that you provided documents from January 1994 also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I am not confirming anything. I am just saying I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have these documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, I do, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that on the 22nd of November, 1995, and the 23rd of February, 1995, you made statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of February, 1995, did you make a statement in the Public Security Station -- Centre of Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No, not in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the Defence is in possession of a statement which says on the 23rd of February, 1995 in the Novi Grad Public Security Centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, if you have the document, it is possible. It was soon after I was wounded so I cannot remember every detail. It is very hard for me. But if it bears my signature, then I will accept it as an official document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In November 1995, you also made the statement to investigators of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the statements you made in the centre of the Novi Grad -- in the Novi Grad Public Security Centre, you described the time and the event that happened in January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I repeat, whatever I said, I abide by it. But I cannot remember all the details after all this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that in 1995, when you made these statements, your memory of these events was better than now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No. I am just talking about my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the event that occurred, can you tell us when your memory was better, in 1995 or now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: It is the same because these events are engraved in one's memory and they are very hard to forget. The intensity of remembering stays the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I put it to you that in the statement you made in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Public Security Centre, you said that on the 21st of January, 1994, you were on your way home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: It is possible, madam, that an error may have occurred. But please try to understand that errors are possible. I allow for the fact that I may have been mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that you allow for the fact that when making your statement in 1995, when you said that this happened on the 21st of January, you were mistaken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Madam I had a difficulty speaking then. I may have been misheard so there may have been an error. The way I speak now is relatively good in relation to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you made a statement on the 22nd of November, 1995, to investigators of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether when you made that statement to the investigators of the Prosecution, you read the statement you had made on the 23rd of February, 1995, in the Public Security station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I put it to you this is your statement of the 22nd of November, 1995. On the first page of that statement, the document number is 00962556 in the original and you say: " I have read the statement I made to the government, to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 23rd of February, 1995, and I confirm that the contents are true to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is your question, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir? Is this correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You saw then that it said in the statement the 21st of January when you read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on the 23rd of February, 1995, you also said that the date when this event occurred was the 21st of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I think the point is perfectly clear. If it is again about a date, that is perfectly clear that there is some contradiction with the date. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what the distance is between phases "B" and "C"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: 150 or 200 metres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you confirm that the address in your medical certificate is an address in phase "C?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you confirm whether in phase "B", on that square, there is a restaurant called "Stela"? I am talking about 1992, 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. I never went into cafes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In phase "B", was there an establishment called "Stela"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the conflict in Sarajevo, 1992, 1993, 1994, in the area of phase "B", there was the headquarters of the 102nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the period from January 1994, specifically on the 21st and 22nd of January, did you see soldiers in that part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in the area of phase "C" there were police stations of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in phase "B", in the part where you lived, the HVO command was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No, and I didn't live in phase "B", I lived in phase "C".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: If you lived in phase "C", do you know that there was a reserve police station in phase "C"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I just said, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "no," are you saying you don't know or that it wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I am saying it wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, 1993 and 1994, given that you told us that you know that Nedzarici was under the control of the army of the Republika Srpska, can you tell us where phase "A" and "B" and their surroundings, can you tell us under whose control these areas were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: You are referring to "A" and "B" phase?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about phases "B" and "C".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: And C, well, they weren't under anyone's control. They were under the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us with regard to Nedzarici which was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska, as you say, and with relation to A, B and C phases, where were the lines of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: As I lived in "C" phase, it was probably behind Vojnicko Polje. I don't know exactly because I am a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict in Sarajevo in 1992, 1993 and 1994, did you have any work duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, I was waiting, as I told you. I was on a waiting list, as I told -- as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness document of the Prosecution 21572. It is a photograph from the 21st of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it has been used before. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please locate the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just enquire of my learned friend, is it 2157 that she said? 2157, that is correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what she said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2172, it says here. Exhibit P2172.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us whether in January, and you spoke about the 22nd of January when my learned colleague put this question to you, you said that the weather was good?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The days preceding that day, was there any precipitation, was there any snow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Perhaps ten days earlier, yes, there might have been snow because there were parts where the children would skate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at photograph number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the document has been admitted under seal, but I do understand that if you just concentrate on the photographs and nothing else, that they could be put on the ELMO, which makes it easier to understand and follow the witness. Yes. If you have a particular photograph. Number two, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, the beginning of "C" phase, there is a square, Alipasino, "C" phase.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of this photograph, can you see some houses in the direction of this red car and in front of a car? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Buildings on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the direction of the buildings, there are cars which can be seen. At the bottom of the photograph, can you see a hill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, the Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know under whose control the Mojmilo hill was in 1992, 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Under the territory of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the BH army was on that hill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you lived for a long time in that part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When my learned colleague asked you this question, you said that shelling was frequent in that part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us in which period this occurred most frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: You mean the time period?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: 1992, 1993 and 1994, these are the years I am thinking of. So before the shelling that you are speaking of now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "every day," could you single out any particular incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. This was something that happened on a daily basis in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "on a daily basis in Sarajevo," could you tell us whether as a result of this shelling that you have been speaking about, whether there were any victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us -- could you mention the name of someone you know who was a victim of shelling in the part in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Someone I knew died.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when this happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us in which month, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I think it was in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have spoken to us today about the fact that you heard the sound of the third shell; you heard the third shell being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you also heard that shell exploding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, on my left-hand side, behind my back.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you distinguish between the firing of a shell and the explosion of a shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, could you describe what the sound is when a shell is being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I tried to explain this to the Prosecutor. Well, it is like the sound made when you open a bottle, you know, it is something like that. But it is a lot louder; the sound is a lot louder.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that on the basis of the shell being fired, you determine which direction the shell had come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you heard, as you said, the sound of the shell being fired, are you quite sure that it was from the direction of Nedzarici or was this just an assumption?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the sound of the first two shells being fired, the first two shells you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear where those two shells exploded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I heard that explosion to my left-hand side, but I couldn't say where exactly. I couldn't pinpoint the location. There were buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us at what distance with regard to the -- from what distance with regard to the place where you were that you heard these shells being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I don't know. As the crow flies, perhaps 100, 150 metres. It is very difficult to determine this precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After this incident occurred, the one you have been speaking about and in which you were wounded, up until the 23rd of February, 1994, did you speak to anyone about that incident? When I say, "to anyone," did you make a statement to the competent authorities? Did you report this incident to those in authority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No, just the statement that I made. I didn't speak to anyone else about the incident. Not the incident, but the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to the Dobrinja hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long you stayed in the Dobrinja hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: They -- they sent us to the Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that in the Dobrinja hospital, you weren't provided with any sort of medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement of the 23rd of February, 1995, you said that in Dobrinja, in the Dobrinja hospital, "I was provided with first aid."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Well, when I say "first aid," that includes an examination, a sort of visual examination to determine whether it is possible to treat him there or not. It depends on how serious the injuries are.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are now telling us you were examined there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes, I was visually examined. When they saw my jaw and my face, well, it was natural for them to send me to the place where they should have sent me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were taken to the surgery department, is that part of the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, part of the UMC, the university medical centre, and the facial surgery department.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long you stayed in the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: The first time, it was a month and-a-half or so, and the second time about two, two and-a-half months, maybe three. Something like that. Well, there are medical records about this in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it is time for a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that you need some more time? You have --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to consult my colleague with regard to the documents which he examined while I was conducting the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Comparing the time you have taken until now, it is just a few minutes less than the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, wouldn't it be better that you now resume your cross-examination and that we deal with the admission of evidence of the documents after we finish the examination of this witness. This also means that if there were any objections against newly provided document P1675.2, that we wait just for ten minutes or quarter of an hour to deal with that and first resume the cross-examination of the witness. Yes, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in 1992, were you a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you possess documentation on the date of your admission to the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the date of admission is on the document that you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: The 22nd of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hand this document over to representatives of the Prosecution when they talked to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has no further questions. My co-counsel wishes to put a few questions relating to documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am not going to ask any questions, but perhaps we could just wait. If Mr. Stamp wants to complete his list of questions and then, after, we will present these questions with regard to the admissibility of these documents in question, with regard to whether or not they should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is not questions but argument on the admissibility of the document. Mr. Stamp, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. AI, I have one question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You might have noticed that when you said that you recognised the document that was shown to you in relation to your treatment, you may have noticed that there was some exchange of views as to the back side of that document where we could, although not easily, discover a few things. Do you know or do you remember what is on the -- if there is anything on the back side of the document and what is on the back side of the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AI
utterances.text: On the front side of the document, it says that I was to report for a check-up in 15 days. On the back of the letter of discharge, it says: "situation unchanged, check-up in 15 days." And then again it says: "situation unchanged, condition unchanged, report back in a month." I think there are two or three of these entries when I went to check-ups with Dr. Piranic. And he would say, "Condition unchanged, next check-up in a fortnight." "Condition unchanged, next check-up in a month." That is what was on the back of this letter of discharge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Mr. AI, you have answered all the question by the parties for the Prosecution, by the Defence, and also by the Bench. It is important for us to hear the answers from those who have been present at the relevant times and at the relevant places because it will assist us in performing our task. Thank you very much for coming and assisting the Tribunal by your presence and by answering these questions. I know it is quite a long trip from Sarajevo to The Hague. I hope you have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, then, would you please escort Mr. AI out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it might be the wisest thing to do is first to deal with the document tendered in respect of Mr. AI and then go back in the past and see what is left from last Friday and even before.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3682, pseudonym sheet under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2183A, discharge -- form letter of discharge in B/C/S. P2183A.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for interrupting you, Madam Registrar. That is always unwise to do, as I know by now. No, no, no, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please, I take it that you want to raise objections against the admittance -- the admissibility of 2183.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am verifying the transcript. I wouldn't want us to have the same problem with numbers that we had on Thursday, because I can see that on several occasions, document 2183 was referred to in the transcript of the hearing -- it is correct now, but just a minute ago, it was 283. This error seems to have been corrected now, but I didn't want us to have the same difficulties. Yes. However that may be, the reason for which we are raising an objection to the tendering of this document is that this document wasn't provided to us in its entirety. The entire document wasn't provided to us, and this is not the first time this has happened. And I have to say that the Defence is quite surprised to come to the conclusion that even on one of these documents -- although on one of these documents we can perfectly well see that the front of the document has writing on it and contains indications. Well, the Defence is surprised to see that it is only part of the document which was provided to it. I am not talking of what has happened today, of course, because we have a copy which is more or less complete. I am referring to documents that we had for this witness and which were provided to us earlier on. Mr. President, it is not just that we were only provided with a partial document, but in addition, at the time we only received a very rudimentary translation, although the Latin was quite elegant. I can see that in the translation that we were provided with, many things were missing. For example, this is just one example, these Latin words. If we have a look at the English translation which we were given today, Mr. President, I can see that yet again certain things have not been translated. And it would suffice to know, as we were reminded by the Trial Chamber, we can see here that we have some numbers which go from 1 to 4 and then pass on to 6 and 7, and this means that, yet again, one or two of the cases at the bottom of the document was not translated. You will also see that in the part which mentions the number of days spent in the hospital, this part has not been translated and there is another part of the document, at the top of this one, here you can read "Odjeljenje-odsjek," and these words have not been translated either. It seems that this has not been translated in the translation that we have just receive from the Prosecution. And when reading through this document again, I can see that a Serbian expression which is on the right below the part, the printed part, and which says "Sifra," this has been translated differently. The English translation is different. I am saying that this is apparently so because I am examining this right now. So to be brief, on the one hand, the document has not been provided, the original document has not been provided, and on the other hand, part of the text has not been translated, and thirdly, with regard to what has been presented to us as a translation, we can see that yet again certain things that are contained in the document have quite simply not been translated, whereas it is quite obvious -- well, we don't have the translation of what was not reproduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you -- I think you assisted the Chamber greatly by pointing at those parts where it seems that the pre-printed text in boxes is not translated, such as the number of days and the -- there were some other entries, for example, the fifth entry between "examined" and the "seised." I do understand that both the accused and the Defence team all read and understand B/C/S. Could you please tell the Chamber in what way the incorrect translation is hindering you in your Defence? So I am not talking about the authenticity, but just about the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, willingly, Mr. President, because, as I said, the Defence is not just a two-headed body and there are people who -- and this is what I could call my support base, there are some people who would like to clarify certain things. This is necessary. And these people only work on the basis of the translations that they are provided with since, contrary to Mr. Galic, they don't speak Serbian. And I rely on them because I have to rely on someone. And if we are provided with incorrect translations, then obviously what results from these translations will be inexact or, at least, this could happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there members belonging to the Defence team who do not understand B/C/S or do not read B/C/S, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in Geneva, there are people who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there aren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question just related to those who were official members of the Defence team. But I do understand that some people who support you might have difficulties when they rely just on the translation and cannot read the original. Is there anything else you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. To reply to your question, Mr. President, whatever the knowledge of languages that my colleagues have, that my colleague has and that General Galic has, it is obvious that the fact that they do know these languages doesn't affect the fact that when certain pages are not translated, which is the case with this document, in that case, we can't know what there is, what it means, and as a result, it is not possible to organise a defence. There is nothing else, apart from the fact, Mr. President, that on page 26 of the transcript, of the French transcript, it would be better to read "investigator," rather than "investors of the Prosecution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, here is a piece of yellow paper which you can use to bring those smaller details to the attention of those who are preparing the transcript, as I told you before. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. an opportunity, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, or Ms. Pilipovic, to check the documents just provided to you? 1675.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, not yet. I was concentrating on other things. I will do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the next break. May I remind the Prosecutor's Office that when this document was discussed before, that they have decided not to tender the documents P1675 and P1675.1 at that time due to the fact that there was no full translation. So I take it now that you do tender all three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would make more sense to tender only .2, that is the fresh translation, but to give it that separate number so as to distinguish it from the earlier translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what it means is the Prosecution now tenders P1675 and 1675.2. Then we still have to deal with two other documents. The first document is -- let me just have a look. That is the meeting which is footnote, I think it was 83, in the report of Mr. Donia. The document as being a part of the footnote materials of the report of Mr. Donia is admitted into evidence. We do not take separate decisions on several parts. It has been used by Dr. Donia to prepare his report. Admitting it into evidence allows the Chamber to check carefully whether the conclusions drawn, from whatever documents supporting the expert report, can be followed or not be followed. Apart from that, there has been extensive cross-examination specifically on this document and that is another reason why we would -- why we admit the documents into evidence. Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the last document is D101. I hardly dare to ask you about completeness of documents, but from the translation I take it that you have not tendered the whole article because the translation ends with a -- with a question without an answer. If I compare it with the original language, I also see that -- at least it appears to me that it is also a question with which the article ends. Is it the whole article or part of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must admit that it is a matter for which I was absent, so Ms. Pilipovic will be in a position to reply to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is just part of the document, part of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was your intention, to just tender part of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we decide that the document is admitted into evidence. At the same time, we see that it's, I would say, double hearsay, and it might be about a different date. But at least it has the probative value that someone says that someone else told him that on a different day, but quite close to the day the expert report deals with, there had been shooting at a crowd from a unit or persons related to Juka Prazina. So, as you may have noticed, in this Chamber and the Tribunal rather liberal rules of admission of evidence do exist. That is because we are not in a jury trial here and that the Chamber will assess what exactly the probative value of the evidence will be at the end of the trial. Having dealt with the documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I be excused, Mr. President? The next witness will be taken again by Mr. Stamp. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I advise that the Prosecution is unable to bring forth the next witness today. As I mentioned in my last letter, we had been liberal perhaps in estimating the time Witness AI would take and we had also decided, having regard to his difficulty in speaking for long periods of time, to try to confine his testimony only to precise issues and not take him into general matters. And it has taken a much shorter time than we expected. He had been set down for two hours, two hours in chief and cross-examination, and with the time that we would have expected to be taken with ancillary applications, he would have taken all of today. That was indicated in our last letter. He has been much shorter and we are not in a position to call any other witnesses today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I am somewhat surprised because, for the 22nd of April, we were told there would be a witness for two hours and that was very short, and everyone is happy about that. But tomorrow, apparently, we won't have anyone, if I can see the programme that the Prosecution provided us. But for the 24th and 25th, if I can see this correctly, we will just have one witness and he has been given one hour. And I would comply with this, but perhaps we should perhaps be told how this shall develop because, two days for one hour for one witness, the figures don't add up. What I can see here, given that there is nothing, I don't know if we are working tomorrow or not but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we are not working tomorrow. That is not because of the Prosecution but because of the Bench. What I see is for the 24th until the 26th of April, that is three days, three witnesses. What is the use of telling us that it is one hour for two days if you see that the next witness is two hours for one of those two days as well and one of those days filled with the last witness. So I have three witnesses for three days, which is the average. But I would, of course, be glad if the average could even be improved without any loss of quality. Mr. Stamp, I take it that not even later today -- if you say not today, that means the witness will not arrive. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And having regard to what you just expressed, Mr. President, the witnesses for the rest of the week have been -- the number of them is deliberately conservative. In fact, there were five other witnesses scheduled, but having regard to difficulties in travelling of one of those witnesses, we had to remove two of them. And we did not want to take a risk that there would be any overlap between civilian witnesses coming from Sarajevo for the next succeeding week which we will not sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It may well be that we will have a shortened week. I don't know if it is wise to try to get another witness and take the risk of having that witness wait here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is always very difficult to strike a fair balance between what is involved in losing a couple of hours in court and, at the same time, what it involves if a witness has to wait for one or two days and has to arrive earlier and then to wait. So I would say until now this Chamber, although it has been announced a few times that we might run out of witnesses, this is actually the first time we really do, and I must say that after three months of trial, that is not a bad performance. I think we are, in general, using our time good. We hardly lose any hours on witnesses who are not available. So I would continue to rely on the -- on what the Prosecution has done until now. Of course, it is difficult for us if you take only 37 minutes, like you did today, where you indicated two hours, of course, for us, it is very difficult to foresee where your initial estimate might not be finally valid any more. So I leave it up to you and I -- the Chamber trusts that in a similar way as you did before, you are taking a -- taking into consideration all the elements, that means waiting of witnesses, efficient use of time in court, et cetera. So I will try to leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Since we find ourselves with some additional time today, I would like to take this opportunity to raise a matter in closed session in relation to the timetable of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could do it right away, I think. So could we please turn into closed session. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 11.55, p.m.,to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
